title: Nepal plans safe resettlement for Bhotekoshi flash flood victims - indiatoday.in
description: Nepal plans safe resettlement for Bhotekoshi flash flood victims  indiatoday.in
publisher.title: indiatoday.in
full_article:
Nepal on Monday said it is in talks with local authorities to resettle victims of the Bhotekoshi flash floods in safe places, as most of them cannot return to the areas where they were living before the disaster. The government said relief, relocation and reconstruction for those affected were being taken up in coordination with different agencies.

Minister for Information and Communication Bikram Timilsina said relocation and reconstruction were among the government’s priorities, and programmes were being moved forward based on the problems faced by the victims and their needs. The issue came up during his meeting at the ministry with a delegation of the Non-Resident Nepali Association, or NRNA.

Flash floods that began near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal. The Bhotekoshi River, which flows south from the Himalayan border region, carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.

According to Timilsina’s secretariat, the minister said, “There is no condition to make settlement for the flood victims in the place where they were living. To develop a new settlement, discussions are going on with the local levels as to which places are safe and appropriate.”

title: Married at 14, a young mother in Nepal now has nowhere to go - The Kathmandu Post
description: Married at 14, a young mother in Nepal now has nowhere to go  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
At 14, Naina (name changed) ran away from home to marry. Now, before turning 20, she is a mother of two daughters and facing pressure from her husband’s family to end her marriage.

But divorce would not necessarily give her a way out.

She has no education to fall back on, no independent income and, because she eloped as a child, little support from her own family. Her parents have stopped speaking to her. Her husband has grown increasingly distant since moving to Kathmandu to study. At home, she says, she has faced repeated abuse, including being blamed for having two daughters instead of a son.

“I have no one to talk to from my parents’ side either. Where am I supposed to go now? I have two daughters and no education?” said Naina, whose name has been changed to protect her privacy.

She has twice gone to the police seeking help over the abuse. On both occasions, she says, the response ended with a written agreement asking the couple to reconcile.

“They make us sign an agreement and send me home. Once I return, the same behaviour starts again,” she said.

Naina’s dilemma is increasingly familiar in rural Achham, where girls who marry before adulthood can find themselves leaving school, becoming pregnant before their bodies are fully mature and entering marriages in which they have little power to make decisions about their health or future.

For some, the consequences are physical. For others, they include violence, pressure to have sons and eventually divorce. Many face several of these at once.

Health officials say the pattern is especially worrying because pregnancy itself can expose adolescent mothers to serious health risks.

Data from the Achham District Health Office show that 3,005 girls under 20 became pregnant in the six years from fiscal 2020-21 to 2025-26. During the same period, 362 babies were stillborn across the district.

title: Brown-affiliated physician and scholar organizes emergency care in Nepal, including for flood victims - Brown University
description: Brown-affiliated physician and scholar organizes emergency care in Nepal, including for flood victims  Brown University
publisher.title: Brown University
full_article:
PROVIDENCE, R.I. [Brown University] — When a devastating flash flood roared through the Himalayan valleys on the Nepal-China border in late August, Dr. Ramu Kharel was in Providence, where he works in the emergency medicine departments of Miriam, Rhode Island and Women and Infants hospitals. Yet Kharel was able to get help to flood survivors in Nepal from thousands of miles away — through his nonprofit, Health Advancement Programs to Serve All (HAPSA) Nepal, Kharel’s team organized the delivery of post-disaster sanitation kits for people who needed them.

“Our organization doesn't have any role in rescue operations — that’s the domain of the army and the government,” Kharel said. “But we know from experience and training that a flood of this magnitude will mean that hundreds of thousands of people will be displaced. And when they get displaced, usually within a week or two, they need a different kind of immediate emergency assistance.”

Kharel is an assistant professor of emergency medicine, clinician educator, at Brown University’s Warren Alpert Medical School, and an affiliated faculty member with the Center for Human Rights and Humanitarian Studies at Brown’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs. His primary research interest is advancing emergency care in Nepal. Kharel founded HAPSA Nepal in 2013 as a handwashing initiative in a rural Nepaleses village, and the organization has since grown to strengthen the chain of emergency care across the country’s health system, often collaborating with local governments during emergencies like earthquakes and floods.

title: Nepal floods show why climate forecasts must improve - Korea JoongAng Daily
description: Nepal floods show why climate forecasts must improve  Korea JoongAng Daily
publisher.title: Korea JoongAng Daily
full_article:
Ha Kyung-ja



The author is an executive director of the APEC Climate Center and professor emeritus at Pusan National University.







Wednesday will mark one month since catastrophic flooding struck Nepal after a massive glacier and rock collapse near Langtang Lirung in the Himalayas, close to the Nepal-Tibet border, at an altitude of about 5,200 meters (17,060 feet).

The collapse was powerful enough to generate seismic waves equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. The resulting flood killed 1,451 people, while 6,150 remain missing, including nine Koreans, according to Nepalese statistics.

While Nepal suffered enormous human and economic losses from a glacier collapse and flooding associated with global warming, the Panama Canal on the other side of the world has faced severe drought. Falling water levels have restricted ship traffic, raising logistics costs and disrupting global supply chains.

Such extremes vividly illustrate the climate crisis confronting the world. Climate change is no longer simply an environmental issue. Its consequences increasingly threaten the global economy, food security and ultimately human survival.

Against this backdrop of growing climate variability, attention is turning to the strengthening El Niño in the equatorial eastern Pacific, east of the International Date Line. The World Meteorological Organization and major climate forecasting models predict that El Niño will intensify further during the second half of this year.

El Niño and La Niña, which can trigger abnormal weather patterns around the world, interact with changes in atmospheric pressure across the tropics. Scientists call this vast coupled ocean-atmosphere system the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, or ENSO.

Its behavior and effects are becoming more complicated as the warming trend in the tropical Pacific interacts with multidecadal fluctuations in ocean temperatures. The crucial question is therefore not El Niño itself but how far in advance we can anticipate its climatic consequences and prepare for them.

The APEC Climate Center, or APCC, provides scientific climate forecasts to help Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation member economies prepare for climate threats. But policy support is essential if scientific diagnosis and forecasting are to translate into effective responses.

To protect Korean society and the economy against a stronger El Niño, I propose three priorities.

First, Korea must substantially improve climate forecasting accuracy while diversifying forecasts to meet the needs of government and industry. Forecasting periods and methods should become more varied so climate information can be useful in real-world settings.

Forecasts should also go beyond temperature and precipitation to include variables such as solar radiation, soil moisture and wind speed. That would allow tailored climate information for purposes including food security, forest protection and energy reserves. Government and businesses should incorporate such information into policies and risk-management systems.

Second, Korea needs ultrahigh-resolution climate forecasting capable of reflecting local terrain, including individual mountains and valleys, supported by adequate computing infrastructure.

Unlike weather forecasts, which focus on short-term changes, climate forecasts deal with longer-term trends. To become genuinely useful on the ground, they must provide far more detailed information at the local level.

Accurately identifying climate variations caused by terrain, such as narrow valleys, could help determine in advance how much wildfire risk or the likelihood of localized torrential rainfall will increase in a particular area during the coming season. That could help prevent crop losses and other damage.

Analyzing such vast quantities of locally tailored climate data quickly and accurately requires proactive national investment in high-speed climate forecasting computing systems.

Third, Korea should establish a permanent system of collaborative production between climate-information providers and those who use the information in the field.

Climate experts and end users must communicate continuously to find the most effective applications. Researchers need sustained exchanges with practitioners in climate-sensitive fields such as disaster prevention, agriculture and water management to develop tailored solutions to practical problems.

Climate forecasting should also be incorporated proactively into macroeconomic and supply-chain risk management. It could help detect potential disruptions to maritime logistics and allow companies and policymakers to diversify sources of imported raw materials before a crisis develops.

Climate disasters are becoming harder to treat as isolated events. Better forecasts alone cannot eliminate their risks. But more accurate, localized and practically useful climate information can give governments, industries and communities more time to prepare — and turn scientific foresight into concrete resilience.

title: Nepal unlikely to hold donor conference for reconstruction - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal unlikely to hold donor conference for reconstruction  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
There is considerable interest in how the government will raise international funds to reconstruct and rebuild infrastructure and private and public property damaged by last month’s Bhotekoshi floods.

The actual extent of the damage and the cost of reconstruction will be known only after the government completes its post-disaster needs assessment (PDNA). The government, however, has already begun preparations to mobilise funds.

According to a rapid damage needs assessment released in the first week of this month, Nepal will require Rs721.31 billion, or approximately $5 billion, for reconstruction. The National Planning Commission has been entrusted with preparing the PDNA, and its report is expected within a month.

Some development partners, including the World Bank and the European Union, have been providing technical and other support for the PDNA.

Following the 2015 earthquake and the completion of the PDNA, the then government organised a donor conference in Kathmandu, bringing together bilateral and multilateral donors to mobilise funds for reconstruction.

This time, however, the mood within the government and the Finance Ministry appear to be leaning towards bilateral negotiations with major donors, according to ministry officials.

“This time, we want to generate funds through bilateral negotiations with major donor countries like India, China, the US, Japan, South Korea, European nations, and others,” a senior Finance Ministry official said. “With multilateral donors like the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, International Monetary Fund and others, we prefer bilateral negotiations rather than organising a donor conference.”

There has been no formal decision yet, but funds could be generated through bilateral negotiations and correspondence, said Amrit Lamsal, head of the International Economic Relations Division at the Finance Ministry.

In this connection, Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle visited India and returned on Saturday after meeting his Indian counterpart Nirmala Sitharaman, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, and other officials.

During his three-day stay in New Delhi, Wagle thanked India for its support and sought help for reconstruction. Both Jaishankar and Sitharaman assured him that India would decide on its support for Nepal's reconstruction after the PDNA report is released.

In an interview with The Hindu newspaper, Wagle put Nepal's reconstruction needs following the August floods at $4.7 billion to $5 billion over three to five years. He said Nepal suffered about $1.8 billion in direct damage and $900 million in losses, but that rebuilding with greater resilience would require $4.7 billion to $5 billion over the next three to five years.

As the Finance Ministry seeks to mobilise funds through bilateral talks and negotiations, the window for foreign funding in the form of grants and aid is narrowing, leaving Nepal increasingly dependent on concessional and other forms of soft loans.

“We are expecting grants and aid from very few countries, and we expect soft loans and concessional loans from many multilateral donors. This is what international financial architecture is building up. Many donors have cut down the aid and grant portion of their lending process, so we would like to depend on concessional loans,” the Finance Ministry official said.

The August 26 flooding has left at least 1,403 people dead in Nepal, according to the latest government figures, with 6,150 still missing. Post File Photo

Wagle is expected to undertake more bilateral visits in the coming weeks to mobilise funds for reconstruction and seek greater support for climate-vulnerable countries.

He is scheduled to travel to Doha to participate in the 2026 annual meeting of the board of governors of the Beijing-based Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) on September 28 and 29. Nepal is the founding member of the AIIB , New York and has been seeking financing for several infrastructure projects.

During the AIIB meeting and his interactions with counterparts on the sidelines, Wagle plans to highlight Nepal's vulnerability to climate-induced disasters and the growing costs the country faces.

Wagle is also scheduled to travel to New York and Washington DC to meet officials from the World Bank and the UN. The annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group are scheduled to take place in Bangkok from October 12-18, and Wagle plans to participate.

“I will be going to Doha, [for the meeting of the] Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank. From then on, I think I will go to the US—New York and Washington DC—to talk with the World Bank and the United Nations,” Wagle told the Indian news agency ANI.

“In the middle of October, there’s the annual meeting of the Bretton Woods institutions in Bangkok. I will be there,” Wagle said.

A few days ago, speaking to The Post, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said the government would prefer grants and aid over loans for reconstruction, although a formal decision has yet to be made.

“Not taking loans is not a declared policy, but we prefer grants and aid,” Khanal told the Post.

Officials and experts, however, say grants alone are unlikely to cover the cost of reconstruction. Nepal's debt burden also increased significantly after the 2015 earthquake and the subsequent reconstruction drive.

The government also plans to seek support from the global Loss and Damage Fund, arguing that climate change contributed to the severity of the floods. Officials acknowledge, however, that international climate funding alone will not be enough.

“But this is at replacement value. When we build back better, this is going to be in excess of $4.5 billion, $5 billion over a number of years. This will require a lot of international solidarity, international assistance, and we will count on Indian assistance, as Prime Minister Modi conveyed to our Prime Minister Balen Shah when they spoke on the telephone,” Wagle told ANI.

A devastating mountain collapse in the Himalayas has drawn attention to the growing risks of a warming planet. On August 26, 2026, a massive rock-and-ice avalanche near the Nepal-China border triggered a destructive flood. A new scientific assessment links climate change to the conditions that helped destabilize the slope.

The disaster devastated settlements and infrastructure. As recovery efforts continued in September, reports put the death toll above 1,300, with thousands more people missing. The tragedy illustrates how environmental changes high in the mountains can have consequences far beyond the glaciers themselves.

An assessment by World Weather Attribution examined the conditions surrounding the collapse. Researchers identified long-term warming, glacier thinning, and thawing mountain permafrost as factors that may have weakened the slope.

Ice and frozen ground help bind rock and sediment together in high-altitude environments. As temperatures rise, that natural support can deteriorate, leaving unstable terrain more vulnerable to collapse.

The Himalayas are especially sensitive to rising temperatures. Their glaciers feed rivers that sustain communities, agriculture, and ecosystems across South Asia. But warming is reshaping the region’s frozen landscapes, with consequences for the stability of mountain slopes.

In this case, a large mass of rock and ice broke away and rushed downhill, transforming into a destructive flood carrying debris into communities below.

Monitoring unstable slopes, glaciers, and permafrost can help researchers identify areas of growing risk. Improved hazard mapping and early-warning systems may also give communities more time to respond, while careful planning around vulnerable valleys can limit exposure.

Nepal’s tragedy shows why understanding climate change requires looking beyond temperature records. In the Himalayas, a warming climate can alter the physical foundations of the landscape itself. When those foundations fail, the consequences can reach far downstream.

full_article:
A Granville High School graduate and public health educator died in Nepal due to flooding and mudslides.

Mark Allen Cantrell, 51, was an adjunct professor at Duquesne University and a U.S. diplomat with USAID.

He died on August 26 while returning from a spiritual pilgrimage in Tibet.

A Granville High School graduate and public health educator died during deadly flooding and mudslides in Nepal in late August.

Mark Allen Cantrell, 51, was a member of Granville High School’s class of 1993, according to an email to The Dispatch by his friend Nicholas Jackson of Newark. Duquesne University, where Cantrell was an adjunct professor, confirmed his death in an email to the university community.

Cantrell died Aug. 26 while returning to Nepal after completing a Yatra, a spiritual pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, according to Duquesne’s student newspaper, The Duquesne Duke. He had initially been listed as missing by Nepal Police.

Jackson contacted The Dispatch to share news of Cantrell’s death and described him as a great friend with a deep commitment to public health.

"I just thought it would be good to do a write-up on Mark and his many accomplishments and love for public health," Jackson said.

Born Feb. 25, 1975, Cantrell joined Duquesne in 2021 as the university’s director of public health. He left the position after about a year to work as a U.S. diplomat with the U.S. Agency for International Development, commonly known as USAID, but continued teaching at Duquesne as an adjunct professor.

Cantrell’s colleagues and former students remembered him as an approachable mentor, passionate educator and avid traveler who incorporated lessons from communities around the world into his teaching.

Cantrell traveled internationally through organizations including USAID and the World Health Organization, bringing what he learned about local health care systems into the classroom. His colleagues said he was particularly interested in creating educational experiences that allowed students to learn directly from different communities.

The Dispatch is working to learn more about Cantrell’s life and his connections to central Ohio. Anyone who knew Cantrell and would like to share memories may contact reporter Amani Bayo at abayo@dispatch.com.

title: Nepal’s Floods Are Putting Women and Girls at Greater Risk - feminist.org
description: Nepal’s Floods Are Putting Women and Girls at Greater Risk  feminist.org
publisher.title: feminist.org
full_article:
As devastating floods continue to affect communities across Nepal, women and girls are facing increased risks of hunger, violence, exploitation, and displacement.

On August 26, a devastating flash flood struck Nepal, destroying homes, roads, bridges and critical infrastructure across several regions near the Nepal-Tibet border. More than 500 people have been killed, nearly 1,000 remain unaccounted for, and around 10,000 homes have been destroyed. But as the communities respond to the disaster, women and girls are facing additional challenges.

According to UN Women, 157,050 women and girls in the districts of Rasuwa and Nuwakot have been affected by the floods. The organization has warned that the disaster is increasing existing risks of violence and exploitation while limiting access to health care and other essential services.

Natural disasters do not affect everyone equally and existing inequalities can become more severe when homes, schools, hospitals and other essential services are destroyed. For women and girls who already face barriers to resources, losing access to these services can put their safety and livelihoods at additional risk. Access to food and water is a particular concern. Flooding has damaged infrastructure and disrupted essential services, leaving survivors facing shortages.

Women often carry a disproportionate share of responsibility for caring for children and other family members. During a disaster, unpaid care work can increase while the resources available to families decrease.

Education is also at risk. In communities already experiencing poverty and instability, disruptions to education can have long-term consequences for girls’ futures. Approximately one in three women across the affected districts are illiterate. Limited literacy can make it more difficult to access relief efforts, complete registration services, or independently apply for assistance. During an emergency, when information about food, shelter, health care and financial assistance can be critical to safety, these barriers become even more significant.

Women are also carrying much of the responsibility for supporting their households. About one-third of households in Nepal’s Bagmati Province are headed by women, making women the primary providers for many families. The floods have destroyed homes, businesses and critical infrastructure, leaving these women responsible for supporting their families while rebuilding their lives with fewer financial resources. The destruction has made it harder for women-led households to access income and recover from the disaster. Humanitarian responses must therefore address the specific needs of women and girls.

UN Women is working with the Nepali government, women’s rights organizations, and humanitarian partners to provide essential services and protection. The organization is also supporting a women-led Community Kitchen initiative designed to provide immediate food assistance while creating opportunities for women’s leadership and livelihoods during the recovery process. UN Women has raised $2 million to support women and girls affected by the floods.

The devastation in Nepal will not disappear when the floodwaters recede. Communities will have to rebuild homes, families, and important infrastructure, but recovery must also address the inequalities that existed before the disaster. Women and girls cannot be treated as an afterthought. They need access to safe shelter, food, clean water, health care and education throughout the recovery process. Nepal’s floods demonstrate that disaster relief is not only about rebuilding, but is about making sure that the people who are most vulnerable are not left even further behind.
